items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules of any kind
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires it. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher gave four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue that 'love' as the only criterion is too vague to guide decisions; defenders argue agape has specific content (the New Testament's understanding) that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.

items.title: The Hebrew Bible barely mentions an afterlife
items.claim: What does the Hebrew Bible (the Christian Old Testament) say about heaven and hell?

options.text: It describes both in detail throughout
It mostly speaks of Sheol — a shadowy underworld where the dead exist as shades — with explicit resurrection only in late texts like Daniel 12

items.reveal:
Job 3:13-19, Ecclesiastes 9:5-10 ('the dead know nothing') and the Psalms describe Sheol as a silent underworld common to all the dead. Daniel 12:2 (mid-2nd century BCE) is the clearest explicit resurrection passage — and it's one of the latest books.

By Jesus's time, Pharisees believed in resurrection and Sadducees did not (Mark 12:18-27). Christian heaven and hell as detailed afterlife destinations are largely shaped by intertestamental Jewish apocalyptic literature, Greek thought and later Christian elaboration (Dante most famously).
items.why: Students often assume the afterlife is a 'religious universal'. Within the Abrahamic tradition itself it's a developing idea, with the most familiar version being relatively recent.

items.title: Modern Judaism has three or four main branches
items.claim: What are the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: One unified Judaism with no internal divisions

Orthodox (including Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Conservative (called Masorti in UK); Reform; Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and the role of modernity
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions exist

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Orthodox responses (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging with modern life.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in different ways.
